subject: DI05007011

intro_text.en: Detailed English Unit 2 for GTU DI05007011, effective 2026–27: 8085 architecture and pins, RISC/CISC, multi-core, motherboards, chipsets, buses, SMPS, SATA/NVMe and RAID. Original practice marks are suggested. Hardware practicals require supervision; no physical tests are claimed.

h.en: 2.1.1 Definition and functions of a microprocessor

body.en:
A microprocessor is a programmable integrated circuit that performs the main processing functions of a CPU. It reads instructions, interprets them and controls arithmetic, logic and data-transfer operations. Its behaviour changes when the program changes; it is not a single-purpose calculator circuit.

  • Arithmetic: addition, subtraction and other operations supported by the instruction set.
  • Logic: comparisons and bit operations such as AND, OR and XOR.
  • Data transfer: moving information between registers, memory and I/O.
  • Control: sequencing instructions, branching and responding to interrupts.

Example: in an educational temperature-monitoring system, input circuitry supplies a numerical reading. A processor compares it with a stored threshold and asks an output circuit to show a warning. The processor does not directly measure temperature without an appropriate sensor/interface.

A practical system needs a processor, program/data memory, I/O interfaces, clock, reset and a suitable power supply. Buses connect these functional blocks. The instruction set architecture (ISA) defines programmer-visible instructions and registers; microarchitecture is the internal implementation.

  1. Fetch: the CPU obtains an instruction byte from memory using an address associated with the program counter.
  2. Decode: control logic interprets the opcode.
  3. Obtain operands: required values come from registers, immediate bytes or memory.
  4. Execute and store: the required operation is performed and results/state are updated.

This is a conceptual sequence, not a claim that every instruction uses one clock period. In the 8085, instructions take machine cycles and T-states, and different instructions take different amounts of time.

BasisMicroprocessorMicrocontroller
Typical integrationCPU-oriented; often external memory and peripheral chipsCPU with memory and selected peripherals on one chip
Typical useGeneral-purpose processing or processor-based systemsEmbedded control
Example8085 with external memory/I/OAn embedded controller with flash, RAM and timers

Modern products blur simple boundaries: a system-on-chip can integrate many functions. Identify the actual device rather than assuming every processor needs the same supporting chips.

• A microprocessor executes a stored program; a complete computer includes supporting resources.
  • An opcode specifies an operation; an operand supplies data or identifies where data is found.
  • Clock frequency alone does not give the execution time of every instruction.

The Intel 8085 is a historical 8-bit microprocessor useful for learning CPU organisation. “8-bit” refers to its basic data processing/data-bus width, not its address width.

FeatureMeaning
8-bit ALU and external data busOrdinary data operations handle 8-bit quantities
16-bit address busAddresses 216 = 65,536 byte locations = 64 KiB
40-pin DIP packageMultiplexing helps fit address, data and control signals into the package
Single +5 V supplyThe classic device uses a +5 V supply; use the exact device datasheet for electrical limits
RegistersA, B, C, D, E, H, L, flag register, PC and SP
Interrupt inputsTRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR
Serial I/OSID and SOD, controlled through RIM/SIM
Clock/control integrationOn-chip clock generation circuitry and bus-control functions

Common teaching examples use a 3 MHz processor clock, but speed grades differ. The crystal/input frequency is divided internally for the processor clock; do not assume an arbitrary crystal frequency equals the CPU operating frequency.

The architecture contains an ALU and accumulator, temporary/internal registers, flag register, register array, PC, SP, instruction register/decoder, timing/control, interrupt control, serial I/O control, and address/data buffers.

Registers hold immediate working state. An internal data path transfers values between blocks. Address buffers drive the address lines; multiplexed address/data buffers share AD0–AD7 over time. Timing/control coordinates memory and I/O operations.

Example: to add register B to A, the ALU receives A and B, performs addition, returns the 8-bit result to A and updates relevant flags. It does not automatically store the result to external RAM.

The accumulator A is an 8-bit register central to many arithmetic and logical operations. The ALU performs the operation while A commonly supplies an operand and receives the result. Internal temporary registers support execution and are not all directly available to the programmer.

FlagMeaning after an applicable operation
S — SignCopies result bit D7; relevant to signed interpretation
Z — ZeroSet when the 8-bit result is zero
AC — Auxiliary carryCarry from bit 3 to bit 4, used for decimal-adjust-related processing
P — ParitySet for an even number of 1 bits in the result
CY — CarryReports carry/borrow according to the operation

Worked example: FFH + 01H = 100H. A retains 00H; CY=1, Z=1, S=0, P=1 and AC=1 for this addition. The carry is stored separately from A. Not every instruction changes every flag: data-transfer instructions generally do not update flags.

B, C, D, E, H and L are six 8-bit general-purpose registers. Instructions can use them individually or, where supported, as BC, DE and HL 16-bit pairs. The first-named register is the high byte.

Register/pairExampleInterpretation
B and CB=20H, C=10HBC=2010H
D and ED=30H, E=00HDE=3000H
H and LH=25H, L=40HHL=2540H; often used as a memory pointer

In instructions using M, M means the memory byte addressed by HL, not a separate physical register named M. With HL=2540H, MOV A,M reads the byte at address 2540H into A. It does not put the number 2540H into A.

The program counter (PC) is a 16-bit register used for instruction sequencing. During fetching it advances through instruction bytes; jumps, calls, returns and interrupts can change the sequence. PC is an address, not the instruction itself.

The stack pointer (SP) is a 16-bit register identifying the top of a software-managed stack in external RAM. The stack stores such things as saved register pairs and return addresses. It is not an internal memory array inside SP.

Worked PUSH example: initially SP=3000H, B=12H and C=34H. After PUSH B, 12H is stored at 2FFFH, 34H at 2FFEH, and SP=2FFEH. A matching POP B restores C from 2FFEH and B from 2FFFH, then SP becomes 3000H. Thus the stack grows towards lower addresses. Stack RAM must be valid and must not overwrite program/data accidentally.

A bus is a set of signal lines carrying related information.

Bus8085 characteristicPurpose
Address16 bits; CPU drives addresses during normal CPU bus ownershipSelect a memory location or I/O port
Data8 bits, bidirectionalCarry instruction/data bytes
Control/statusMultiple signals with different directionsIndicate read/write, memory/I/O, readiness and bus ownership

Memory range: 0000H–FFFFH includes 65,536 byte addresses. A 16-bit address bus does not mean 16-bit ordinary data transfers. Isolated I/O instructions use an 8-bit port number; memory-mapped I/O uses memory addresses and consumes part of the memory map.

h.en: 2.2.7 Multiplexing and ALE — separating address from data

body.en:
Pins AD0–AD7 carry low-order address bits A0–A7 during T1, then serve as the data bus during the later part of the machine cycle. Pins A8–A15 carry the high address byte. This saves pins, but external circuitry must preserve the low address while the shared pins carry data.

  1. The CPU outputs the address; ALE indicates the address-latch interval.
  2. An external latch captures A0–A7.
  3. The latch continues to present the captured low address after ALE falls.
  4. AD0–AD7 can now carry a read or write data byte.

Example: for address 2050H, A8–A15 carry 20H and AD0–AD7 initially carry 50H. If the memory byte is A6H, the shared lines later carry A6H during the read. Without a latch the low address would be lost.

• A is 8-bit; PC and SP are 16-bit.
  • BC, DE and HL are supported register pairs; M refers to memory at HL.
  • Address capacity = 216 bytes = 64 KiB, not 64 MB.
  • The ALU computes; the control unit sequences; flags describe applicable results.
  • ALE helps demultiplex AD0–AD7; it is not a data-storage instruction.

/RD asks the selected memory or input device to place data on the bus. /WR asks the selected memory or output device to accept data. Address decoding and status signals determine which device responds; /RD alone does not uniquely select every memory chip.

CycleIO/MS1S0
Opcode fetch011

This table covers ordinary identification examples. Halt, bus-hold and reset conditions require the device timing/status specification rather than extrapolating this table. During an opcode fetch the byte is an instruction opcode; a memory read may instead obtain an operand.

An interrupt requests attention so the CPU can run a service routine. A maskable interrupt can be disabled or masked under the supported rules; a non-maskable interrupt is not controlled by the ordinary interrupt-enable flag.

InputPriorityVector addressTrigger summary
TRAPHighest0024HEdge and level sensitive; non-maskable
RST 7.5Next003CHRising-edge sensitive, latched
RST 6.5Next0034HLevel sensitive
RST 5.5Next002CHLevel sensitive
INTRLowestExternally supplied instruction determines service entryLevel sensitive, non-vectored

RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 support individual masking. /INTA acknowledges an accepted INTR request. SID and SOD are serial input/output data pins associated with RIM and SIM. They are not a complete automatic UART or USB interface.

h.en: 2.3.5 Clock, reset, READY and DMA handshake

body.en:
X1/X2 connect the specified clock network; CLK OUT provides a timing output for supporting circuitry. /RESET IN resets CPU control state and makes execution restart at address 0000H when reset is released according to timing requirements. It does not erase every external RAM location or promise zero in every general register. RESET OUT can reset supporting devices.

READY: a slow memory/peripheral can hold READY low so the processor inserts wait states. This is different from requesting an interrupt.

HOLD/HLDA: an external controller requests the buses using HOLD. After completing the current bus transfer under the device rules, the processor acknowledges using HLDA and releases the relevant buses, allowing direct memory access. A DMA controller still needs valid address, control and arbitration circuitry.

RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer; CISC means Complex Instruction Set Computer. These labels describe broad ISA design traditions, not a guaranteed ranking of speed, power or quality.

BasisTypical RISC tendencyTypical CISC tendency
Instruction designRelatively regular, simpler operationsMore varied operations and addressing modes
Memory operationsLoad/store approach commonSome operations directly use memory operands
EncodingRegular encoding common; compressed forms also existVariable-length encoding common
RegistersOften a larger programmer-visible register setHistorically often fewer; exact ISA matters
ImplementationCan ease regular decoding/pipeliningComplex instructions may be decoded into internal operations
ExamplesArm, RISC-Vx86; 8085 is commonly taught in the CISC tradition

Suppose a value in memory must be increased. In a load/store ISA, the conceptual steps are load into register → add → store back. Another ISA may provide an instruction that updates a memory operand. Exact assembly syntax and instruction count depend on the ISA.

Fewer instructions do not automatically mean less time: an instruction may take more cycles, decode differently or wait for memory. Modern implementations use caches, pipelines, speculation and other techniques. Some x86 implementations decode instructions into simpler internal operations; this does not change the externally visible ISA into a RISC ISA.

Exam approach: define both terms, compare at least four tendencies, give examples and end with “actual performance depends on implementation and workload.” Avoid claims that all RISC instructions take one cycle or that CISC cannot be pipelined.

A core is an instruction-executing processing engine within a processor design. A dual-core processor contains two physical cores; a quad-core contains four. They can make progress on separate instruction streams, subject to software and shared-resource limits.

Cores may have private caches and share other cache levels, memory controllers or interconnects. Exact sharing is model-dependent. Multiple cores in one package differ from multiple CPU sockets. Simultaneous multithreading (SMT) exposes additional logical execution contexts on a core; four logical processors are not proof of four physical cores.

• Parallel work: independent tasks or supported portions of a program may run concurrently.
  • Responsiveness: background work can run while the user interacts with another task.
  • Throughput: a system can complete more suitable tasks in a given time.
  • Efficiency opportunities: work can be distributed across suitable cores, but power savings are not automatic.

Worked example: a job takes 100 seconds on one core; 20 seconds are inherently serial and 80 seconds divide perfectly. On four cores the ideal time is 20 + 80/4 = 40 seconds, giving speedup 100/40 = 2.5×, not 4×. Synchronisation, scheduling and memory contention may reduce the real gain further.

Key point: compare actual workloads, architecture, memory and thermal limits—not only core counts or GHz.

The motherboard is the main printed circuit board that supports and interconnects the processor, memory, expansion devices, firmware and power/control circuits. A functional block diagram explains relationships; a layout shows physical placement. Neither is a universal wiring guide.

A generic modern desktop may connect RAM and a primary PCIe graphics/storage path directly to CPU controllers, while a platform controller hub (PCH) handles additional I/O through a CPU–chipset link. AMD and other platforms may use different names and integration. Consult the exact platform block diagram.

ComponentFunctionIdentification caution
CPU socket/package areaConnects/supports a compatible CPUSocket shape alone does not prove BIOS/CPU support
DIMM slotsConnect compatible RAM modulesDDR generations are not interchangeable
VRM and heatsinksRegulate CPU/component powerDo not touch exposed powered circuitry
Chipset/PCHCoordinates supported I/OMay be covered by a heatsink
PCIe slotsAccept compatible expansion cardsPhysical length may exceed wired lane count
M.2 socketAccepts specified modulesCheck key, protocol, length and lane sharing
SATA portsConnect SATA drives by data cableA drive also needs appropriate power
Firmware flashStores BIOS/UEFI firmwareNot the same as the CMOS battery
Coin cell/RTC supportSupports RTC/settings functions depending on boardNot the main PC power source
HeadersFront panel, fans, USB, audio and other connectionsUse exact manual; pin assignments differ

h.en: 2.6.3 Reading a physical layout and checking compatibility

body.en:
1. Read the exact board model and revision printed on the PCB or label.
  2. Find the CPU socket, DIMM slots, expansion slots, storage connectors and power connectors in the manual.
  3. Check CPU support list and required firmware version.
  4. Check RAM type/capacity, case mounting points, cooler clearance and PSU suitability.
  5. Check shared-lane restrictions: using one socket may disable a port or reduce lanes elsewhere.
  6. Map front-panel power/reset/LED connectors from the manual, not wire colour guesses.

For unpowered visual identification, shut down, isolate external power and follow manufacturer/ESD procedures. A switched-off PC may still have standby power while connected. Do not move components with power present.

A form factor specifies mechanical and associated layout/interface conventions. It is not a processor performance grade.

AT: historical IBM PC/AT-derived boards; full-size AT was roughly 305 × 351 mm, while Baby AT was smaller. Legacy AT systems commonly used paired P8/P9 power connectors and a mechanical mains switch. These are historical recognition topics, not instructions to work on mains wiring.

ATX: commonly 305 × 244 mm for full-size boards, with a defined rear-I/O/expansion arrangement and soft-power control. Modern ATX-derived systems commonly use a 24-pin main power connector plus a separate CPU-power connector. Earlier ATX supplies/boards used 20-pin arrangements. Always check the actual generation.

Form factorCommon maximum/standard sizeExpansion tendencyTypical use
ATX305 × 244 mmMore expansion positions; often more connectorsGeneral/full-size desktop
Micro-ATX244 × 244 mm maximumUp to four expansion positions in the form-factor envelopeCompact/mainstream desktop
Mini-ITX170 × 170 mmUsually one expansion positionSmall-form-factor desktop

Commercial boards may be narrower than their form-factor maximum. Actual RAM slots, M.2 sockets and performance depend on the model. Mini-ITX does not mean a weak processor; it mainly constrains space, expansion and cooling options.

Worked selection: for a compact office PC with one optional add-in card, Micro-ATX or Mini-ITX may suit. For several add-in cards, examine ATX board lane allocation and spacing. A larger case may support smaller boards only when mounting locations and clearances match.

A chipset is supporting control logic for the processor platform. In a traditional two-hub PC design, the northbridge handled comparatively high-speed paths such as CPU–RAM and graphics connectivity. The southbridge handled lower-speed I/O such as storage, USB, firmware interfaces and legacy peripherals, according to the chipset generation.

A simplified path was CPU ↔ northbridge ↔ RAM/graphics, with southbridge connected below the northbridge. “North” and “south” are diagram conventions, not guaranteed physical board positions. They are not parts of the 8085 architecture.

Many modern CPUs integrate the memory controller and some PCIe connectivity. A PCH or related chipset handles additional I/O. Some systems-on-chip integrate still more functions.

QuestionTraditional two-hub exampleCommon modern example
Who controls RAM?NorthbridgeCPU-integrated memory controller
Primary graphics pathNorthbridge AGP/PCIe pathOften CPU PCIe lanes
Other I/OSouthbridgePCH/chipset or SoC
Important limitationGeneration-dependent featuresCPU–chipset link bandwidth can be shared by several devices

Example: two fast drives attached through the chipset may share the chipset uplink. Their advertised individual maximum rates do not guarantee both can sustain those rates simultaneously. Platform manuals identify the actual connections.

An expansion bus connects additional functions such as graphics, network, sound or storage controllers. A slot is a physical connector; electrical signalling and protocol determine compatibility.

TechnologyOrganisationTypical historical purpose / caution
ISALegacy parallel shared bus; 8-bit/16-bit versionsOlder expansion cards; obsolete for normal modern desktops
PCIParallel shared bus, commonly 32-bit; other variants existNetwork, sound and other cards
PCI-XParallel PCI-derived server/workstation technology, commonly 64-bitNot PCI Express; check voltage/keying and variant support
PCI Express (PCIe)Serial point-to-point links made of lanesModern graphics, network, storage and other expansion
AGPDedicated parallel graphics interfaceLegacy graphics slot; not compatible with PCIe graphics cards
USBHost-managed serial bus through hubs/portsExternal peripherals and some internal headers; not a PCIe card slot
VESA Local Bus (VLB)Legacy parallel local bus closely associated with 486 systemsOlder graphics/storage expansion; often physically extends a slot arrangement

A PCIe lane has separate transmit and receive differential pairs, enabling full-duplex communication. Links commonly use x1, x4, x8 or x16 lane widths. Generation and negotiated width both affect available bandwidth.

A mechanical x16 slot can be electrically wired as x4. A smaller compatible card can often fit a larger suitable slot, but firmware, power, clearance and vendor restrictions still matter. Shared CPU lanes can change widths when multiple cards are installed.

Worked Gen3 estimate: PCIe 3.0 uses 8 GT/s per lane and 128b/130b encoding. Approximate encoded payload capacity before higher-level overhead is 8 × 128/130 ÷ 8 = 0.985 GB/s per lane per direction. For x4 it is about 3.94 GB/s per direction. Application throughput is lower and depends on devices/workload. Do not confuse GT/s with GB/s.

ISA, PCI, PCI-X, AGP and VLB are not interchangeable names. Card length, notches, signalling voltage and protocol differ. Never force a card into a slot or use appearance alone to declare compatibility.

USB connects devices through a host-controlled topology. USB-A, USB-B and USB-C describe connector families; connector shape does not uniquely determine data speed, charging power, display support or Thunderbolt capability. USB is included in this syllabus bus list, but is not a conventional motherboard add-in card edge slot.

Revision: PCI-X has an X in the name but is not PCIe. AGP was a dedicated graphics path; PCIe serves many device types. VLB is historical, not an alternative name for a modern high-speed interconnect.

A switched-mode power supply (SMPS) converts input power into regulated outputs using high-frequency switching. A desktop PSU accepts mains AC and provides suitable DC rails and control signals.

  1. Input protection/filtering: limits interference and provides protective functions.
  2. Rectification and high-voltage DC stage: converts AC into a DC bus; power-factor-correction circuitry may be included.
  3. High-frequency switching: semiconductor switches control energy transfer.
  4. Isolation/transformer stage: transfers energy with the required isolation in the design.
  5. Secondary rectification/conversion and filtering: produces DC output rails. Modern supplies may derive some rails through DC–DC stages.
  6. Feedback and protection: regulate outputs and respond to relevant abnormal conditions.

High switching frequency permits smaller magnetic components than a simple mains-frequency transformer design. Efficiency is output power divided by input power; a wattage rating is not the power constantly consumed by every PC.

ConnectorNormal roleImportant caution
ATX main 24-pin / 20+4Motherboard main power and control; common legacy rails +3.3 V, +5 V, +12 V, -12 V and +5 V standbyExact pinout/revision matters; not every modern platform uses this design
CPU ATX12V 4-pin / EPS-style 8-pin, often 4+412 V input near CPU VRMNot interchangeable with a PCIe GPU 8-pin cable
PCIe GPU 6-pin / 6+2Auxiliary power for compatible graphics cardsUse PSU/card-approved cables; do not force or substitute CPU leads
Newer high-power GPU connector familiesPower for supported newer graphics cardsFollow exact connector, seating, cable and bend guidance
SATA power 15-pinPower for compatible SATA drivesDifferent from 7-pin SATA data
Legacy peripheral 4-pinOlder drives and selected accessoriesNot the 4-pin CPU-power connector
Modular PSU-side connectorsAttach removable PSU cablesPinouts are not universal even when plugs fit

Soft power: on conventional ATX, the motherboard asserts PS_ON# to request main outputs; the PSU provides PWR_OK when outputs satisfy its required conditions. Standby power can remain present while the PC appears off. A case power button normally signals the motherboard; it is not a mains-isolation switch.

h.en: 2.10.3 Safe SMPS study and measurement limits

body.en:
Never open a PSU enclosure. Internal capacitors may retain dangerous energy after unplugging. Do not bypass protective earth, short unknown pins, perform improvised paperclip tests or probe the mains/primary side.

The syllabus includes a supervised practical measuring SMPS outputs with a digital multimeter. Treat that as an instructor-controlled laboratory activity using a documented, protected low-voltage test setup—not a home experiment. Identify connectors from the exact manual while unpowered; an instructor must approve any powered secondary-side measurements and meter setup.

A voltage reading alone does not prove ripple, load regulation, protection or overall PSU health. A PSU with a spinning fan is not necessarily good. Replace suspect sealed units through qualified service rather than teaching internal repair here.

Serial ATA (SATA) is a serial storage interface used by many HDDs, SSDs and optical drives. A typical desktop SATA drive has separate 7-pin data and 15-pin power connections. The data cable connects a drive to a host port; it does not normally supply the drive’s main operating power.

SATA generations commonly specify 1.5, 3 and 6 Gb/s link rates. SATA 6 Gb/s uses 8b/10b encoding: 6 × 8/10 ÷ 8 = 0.6 GB/s before protocol overhead. Actual application speed is lower. A SATA SSD can outperform an HDD despite using the same interface because the storage medium/controller differs.

Hot-plug support depends on controller, firmware, software and enclosure design. It is not permission to unplug arbitrary internal cables while powered. For ordinary installation follow the manufacturer’s shutdown/isolation procedure.

NVM Express (NVMe) is a storage command/interface architecture designed for non-volatile memory. Common local NVMe SSDs communicate over PCIe. NVMe supports queues and parallel command handling suited to fast storage; it is not simply a faster SATA cable.

M.2 is a module/connector form-factor specification. An M.2 storage module/socket may support SATA or PCIe/NVMe, depending on its implementation. M.2 does not automatically mean NVMe, and NVMe drives also exist in other form factors such as add-in cards and supported 2.5-inch connector arrangements.

CheckReason
ProtocolSATA-only and PCIe/NVMe-only support may differ
KeyingMechanical compatibility does not by itself prove protocol support
LengthA 2280 module is nominally 22 mm wide and 80 mm long; other sizes exist
PCIe generation/lanesNegotiated link can limit throughput
Boot/firmware supportDetection and boot support depend on platform
Lane/port sharingInstalling a module may disable a SATA port or change other links

A typical M.2 NVMe drive plugs directly into the supported motherboard socket and does not use an ordinary SATA data cable. Read the board manual before fitting it.

RAID combines drives into an array using techniques such as striping, mirroring and parity. It is a storage-organisation method, not a physical connector or transport interface. Software or dedicated controllers can implement RAID.

LevelTechniqueMinimum drivesUsable capacity with N equal drives of SFault tolerance
RAID 0Striping2N × SNone; one drive failure can lose the array
RAID 1Mirroring, common two-drive case2S for a two-drive mirrorOne drive in a two-drive mirror
RAID 5Striping with single distributed parity3(N − 1) × SAny one drive
RAID 6Striping with dual distributed parity4(N − 2) × SAny two drives
RAID 10Stripe across mirrored pairs4, typically even(N/2) × SDepends on which drives fail; not any arbitrary two

Capacity formulae ignore filesystem/controller overhead and assume conventional equal-sized arrangements. Mixed drives are often limited by the smallest member in the relevant group. Rebuilds take time, reduce performance and can expose additional failures.

h.en: 2.11.4 RAID worked examples and backup distinction

body.en:
Example 1: four 2 TB drives yield about 8 TB in RAID 0, 6 TB in RAID 5, 4 TB in RAID 6 or 4 TB in conventional RAID 10, before overhead. These use decimal drive capacities; OS display units may differ.

Example 2: RAID 10 has mirrors (A,B) and (C,D). Failure of A and C can be tolerated because B and D remain. Failure of A and B loses one whole mirror and the array fails. Therefore “RAID 10 survives any two failed drives” is incorrect.

RAID is not backup. Accidental deletion, ransomware, corruption, theft and fire can affect the entire live array. Use separate, tested backups appropriate to the risk. Creating/reconfiguring an array may erase existing data: the lesson uses paper calculations only, not instructions to alter a learner’s live disks.

• Explain microprocessor, buses, registers, PC and SP.
  • Draw the 8085 architecture and top-view pin diagram with correct signal names.
  • Explain AD multiplexing and ALE using an address/data example.
  • Compare RISC/CISC and dual/quad-core without absolute speed claims.
  • Identify motherboard components, form factors and traditional/modern chipsets.
  • Distinguish all seven syllabus bus technologies.
  • Describe SMPS stages and connector roles with electrical safety.
  • Distinguish SATA, PCIe, NVMe, M.2 and RAID; solve basic RAID capacity examples.

body.en:

Model answer / answer outline: Both are 16-bit address registers. PC sequences instruction fetching and is changed by branches/calls/returns. SP identifies the stack in RAM. With SP=3000H and BC=1234H, PUSH B stores 12H at 2FFFH and 34H at 2FFEH; SP becomes 2FFEH.

h.en: Practice 6 — Explain multiplexing of AD0–AD7 and the role of ALE.

body.en:
Suggested marks: 4 — original practice, not an official GTU allocation.

Model answer / answer outline: During T1 the shared pins carry A0–A7, captured by an external latch controlled by ALE. They later carry data while the latch maintains the low address. For 2050H the low byte is 50H and high byte is 20H. A later A6H data byte does not change the latched 50H address.

h.en: Practice 11 — Calculate ideal quad-core speedup for 20% serial work.

body.en:
Suggested marks: 3 — original practice, not an official GTU allocation.

Model answer / answer outline: Normalise one-core time to 100 units. Serial part=20; parallel part=80. Four-core ideal time=20+80/4=40; speedup=100/40=2.5. Real overhead can reduce the gain.

q.en: What makes the 8085 an 8-bit processor?

a.en: Its basic ALU/data operations and external data bus are 8-bit; its address bus is 16-bit.

q.en: How much memory can 8085 address?

a.en: 65,536 byte locations, or 64 KiB, from 0000H to FFFFH.

q.en: Name the six general-purpose registers.

a.en: B, C, D, E, H and L.

q.en: What is the accumulator?

a.en: The 8-bit A register, used by many arithmetic/logical instructions for an operand and result.

q.en: What does M mean in MOV A,M?

a.en: The memory byte addressed by HL, not a separate M register.

q.en: What does PC hold?

a.en: A 16-bit address used to sequence instruction fetching.

q.en: Where is the stack stored?

a.en: In external RAM; SP holds the top-of-stack address.

q.en: Which direction does the 8085 stack grow?

a.en: Towards lower memory addresses when data is pushed.

q.en: Name the five flags.

a.en: Sign, Zero, Auxiliary Carry, Parity and Carry.

q.en: Why are AD0-AD7 multiplexed?

a.en: To share pins between the low address byte in T1 and data later, reducing pin count.

q.en: What is ALE used for?

a.en: To control capture of the low address byte in an external latch.

q.en: What does /RD mean?

a.en: Read control asserted at logic 0.

q.en: What is the highest-priority interrupt?

a.en: TRAP, a non-maskable vectored interrupt.

q.en: Is SID/SOD a full UART?

a.en: No. They provide basic software-controlled serial input/output functions.

q.en: Why is READY used?

a.en: To insert wait states for slow memory or I/O when READY is low.

q.en: What is the HOLD/HLDA handshake?

a.en: An external controller requests bus ownership with HOLD; the CPU acknowledges with HLDA under its timing rules.

q.en: Give examples of RISC and CISC ISAs.

a.en: Arm and RISC-V are RISC examples; x86 is a CISC example.

q.en: Are all RISC instructions one-cycle?

a.en: No; timing depends on implementation, instruction and memory/system effects.

q.en: Does quad-core mean four CPU sockets?

a.en: No. It means four physical cores in the processor design.

q.en: Does four logical processors prove four cores?

a.en: No; SMT can expose multiple logical contexts per physical core.

q.en: What is a motherboard form factor?

a.en: Mechanical/layout conventions governing board dimensions, mounting and related arrangements.

q.en: What is the Mini-ITX board size?
What did a traditional northbridge handle?

a.en: High-speed CPU, memory and graphics paths, depending on generation.

q.en: Where is the memory controller in many modern PCs?

a.en: Integrated into the CPU.

q.en: Is PCI-X the same as PCI Express?

a.en: No. PCI-X is a parallel PCI-derived technology; PCIe is serial point-to-point.

q.en: What is a PCIe lane?

a.en: A full-duplex link unit with separate transmit and receive differential pairs.

q.en: Does a full-length x16 slot guarantee x16 wiring?

a.en: No. The slot can be electrically wired for fewer lanes.

q.en: What does USB-C guarantee about speed?

a.en: Connector shape alone does not specify the supported speed, power or optional features.

q.en: Why must a PSU enclosure remain closed?

a.en: Mains-side circuitry and retained capacitor energy can be dangerous even after unplugging.

q.en: Can CPU and PCIe 8-pin power cables be exchanged?

a.en: No; similar appearance does not imply compatible pinouts.

q.en: Can modular PSU cables be reused between arbitrary models?

a.en: No. PSU-side pinouts are not universal.

q.en: What is the difference between SATA data and power?

a.en: Typical desktop SATA data uses 7 pins; SATA power uses 15 pins.

q.en: Is M.2 a synonym for NVMe?

a.en: No. M.2 is a form-factor/connector specification; storage modules may use SATA or PCIe/NVMe.

q.en: Is RAID a storage interface?

a.en: No. It is an array organisation method.

q.en: Does RAID 0 provide redundancy?

a.en: No. A member failure can lose the entire array.

q.en: Why is RAID not a backup?

a.en: It does not independently protect against deletion, ransomware, corruption or site loss.
